stories.headline: Lauren Boebert's Son Arrested on Child Sexual Exploitation Charges in Colorado
stories.summary:
Tyler Boebert, 21, son of U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, was arrested in Colorado on Sunday on suspicion of sexual exploitation of a child, the Garfield County Sheriff's Office announced. He faces five felony charges, including sexual exploitation of a child and sexual exploitation of a child with enticement, with one count also involving a video.

The charges represent a significant legal development for the family of the Republican congresswoman, who represents Colorado's 4th Congressional District. Garfield County, located in western Colorado, is within Boebert's district.

Details about the specific allegations underlying the charges have not been fully disclosed by authorities. The case is being handled by the Garfield County Sheriff's Office.

stories.headline: Five Grand Junction Teenagers Killed After Car Drives Off Cliff Late Saturday
stories.summary:
Five 17-year-old boys died late Saturday night after a vehicle they were in drove off a cliff near 2694 Lookout Lane in Grand Junction, according to the Mesa County Coroner's Office. Grand Junction police and firefighters responded to the scene at about 7:45 a.m. Sunday and found the vehicle crashed on a steep hillside, with all five occupants pronounced dead at the scene.

All five teens were residents of Grand Junction. Three were wearing seatbelts, including the driver and front-seat passenger. The other two were not restrained and were ejected from the vehicle. Investigators believe the car was traveling southbound on Lookout Lane when it veered off the roadway.

Speed is being investigated as a factor in the crash, according to Grand Junction police. The coroner's office said it will not release the names of the minors in keeping with its policy regarding juvenile victims. The incident remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Denver Mayor Mike Johnston Officially Files for 2027 Reelection
stories.summary:
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston filed paperwork Monday to seek reelection in the 2027 mayoral race, formalizing what he had confirmed to the Denver Gazette weeks earlier. Johnston said his focus for the final year of his current term will center on affordability challenges, particularly housing costs, as well as utility costs and childcare.

Johnston's tenure has included bridging a $200 million budget deficit through a hiring freeze, layoffs and furlough days, and spending nearly $200 million on homelessness initiatives. The mayor defended that spending, saying Denver delivered "the largest reduction in street homelessness of anything in American history" and that per-person costs are now lower than before the initiatives began.

Johnston faces a competitive field that includes City Councilmember Shontel Lewis, progressive Lisa Calderón, and six other candidates. The mayor's filing signals the formal start of what is expected to be a contested race ahead of the spring 2027 election.

stories.headline: State Health Officials Warn of Public Health Order as Aurora ICE Facility Blocks Tuberculosis Investigation
stories.summary:
Colorado state health officials said a public health order remains "on the table" after operators of the Aurora ICE detention facility have continued to block state investigators from completing a tuberculosis investigation. The standoff raises concerns about the potential spread of a communicable disease within the detention population and among staff.

The Aurora facility, which houses immigration detainees, has been the subject of ongoing scrutiny regarding health and safety conditions. State officials have not yet detailed the scope of the potential TB exposure or the number of individuals who may have been affected.

A public health order would give state authorities legal authority to compel access to the facility for investigative purposes. The situation marks an escalation in the conflict between state public health authorities and federal immigration detention operators.

stories.headline: Colorado Wolf Killed by Hunter Who Mistook It for Coyote, CPW Announces
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife announced Monday that a female gray wolf from the state's reintroduction program was shot and killed in January by a licensed hunter who believed the animal was a coyote. The hunter shot the wolf on Jan. 16 in the northwest region of the state and promptly reported the incident to CPW, cooperating fully with the subsequent investigation.

CPW cited the hunter for violating agency regulations — specifically, killing an animal without the appropriate license — which carries a $140 fine and suspension points against the hunting license. Authorities said they will not pursue further charges, citing the hunter's immediate self-reporting and cooperation as mitigating factors.

The wolf, identified as female wolf 2504, was one of 15 animals captured in Canada and released into Colorado in January 2025. Gray wolves remain a state and federally protected species. The death brings the total number of wolves lost since reintroduction began in 2023 to 17, and is the third wolf shot and killed in Colorado by someone other than CPW staff.

stories.headline: Colorado State Patrol Trooper Airlifted After 4-Vehicle Crash at Eisenhower Tunnel
stories.summary:
A Colorado State Patrol trooper was airlifted to a hospital Monday after a four-vehicle crash near the Eisenhower Tunnel on Interstate 70, according to the agency. The trooper was parked on the right shoulder of eastbound I-70 at about 10:45 a.m. when he heard a crash in the westbound lanes over the radio, activated his emergency lights, and began turning across traffic to respond — at which point he was struck by an eastbound Subaru Forester SUV.

The collision sent the trooper's vehicle and the Subaru across the highway median, where they struck two pickup trucks in the westbound lanes. The Subaru's occupants, described as an elderly couple, were transported to a hospital with unknown injuries. No one in the pickup trucks was injured. Buck, a police dog riding with the trooper, was taken to a veterinarian as a precaution.

Westbound I-70 was closed for several hours before reopening at 5:10 p.m., while eastbound lanes reopened shortly before 1:45 p.m., according to the Colorado Department of Transportation. The Colorado State Patrol is asking anyone with information to contact investigators at 303-239-4501, referencing case number VC260276.

stories.headline: Denver International Airport Launches Global CEO Search, Aims for Nomination by Year-End
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport has engaged global executive search firm Korn Ferry to conduct a worldwide search for a new chief executive officer, the Denver Business Journal reported. Mayor Mike Johnston is expected to make a nomination by the end of the year.

DIA is one of the busiest airports in the United States and a major economic driver for the Denver metro region. The leadership transition comes as the airport continues capital improvement projects and navigates ongoing passenger growth.

The timeline signals that DIA could enter 2027 with new executive leadership. The global scope of the search suggests city officials are considering candidates from outside the Denver market.

stories.headline: Golden Triangle Neighborhood Set to Gain Its First New Park in 15 Years
stories.summary:
Denver City Council voted 8-5 last week to approve a $3.2 million purchase of a lot at 1028 N. Acoma St. in the Golden Triangle neighborhood to be developed into a 0.4-acre park, the first new green space the area has seen in nearly 15 years. The Golden Triangle sits in the city's 10th council district, which has the least park space per resident of any district — just 2.3 acres per 1,000 residents, compared to a citywide average of 9.4 acres.

The purchase price is approximately $500,000 above the appraised value of the property, a point of contention for five council members who voted against the deal. Councilwoman Amanda Sandoval cited the above-appraisal cost, while Councilwoman Amanda Sawyer said she supported the project but is frustrated with the parks department's struggles to maintain services in her own district.

The lot was formerly a credit union owned by local developer Fred Glick. Funding will come from Denver's Parks Legacy Fund, approved by voters in 2018 through a 0.25% sales and use tax increase. The park is expected to open in a few years and will serve a neighborhood that is adding thousands of new housing units through ongoing vertical development.

stories.headline: Block Distilling Co. in RiNo to Close After Nearly a Decade
stories.summary:
The Block Distilling Co., located at 2990 Larimer St. in Denver's River North Arts District, announced it will close later this year after nearly a decade in operation. The distillery did not give a specific closing date, but said on social media it would host events over a three-to-four-month wind-down period.

Owners Kraig, Michelle, and Kameron Weaver opened The Block in late 2017, building a following for its gin, whiskey, and more unusual spirits such as pear brandy, coffee liqueur, and various amaros. The distillery's seasonal cocktail taproom and distinctive square glass bottles made it a recognized presence on Colorado store shelves. The Denver Post named it one of the hottest places to drink in Colorado in 2024.

The owners cited "timing" and broader trends in the spirits industry in their closing announcement, noting that "the industry is in the dumps." The closure follows a period of consolidation and difficulty across Colorado's craft spirits sector. Bottle discounts and one-off releases are planned during the wind-down.

stories.headline: Longmont's First Boutique Hotel Opens; New Seafood Restaurant Coming to Denver Tech Center
stories.summary:
Hotel Longmont opened last week at 508 3rd Ave. in downtown Longmont, becoming the city's first boutique hotel. The 84-room property, developed by Mississippi-based The Thrash Group and Colorado-based Vertikal, includes a rooftop restaurant and bar called Longmont Supply, 3,700 square feet of meeting space, and a ballroom that can accommodate up to 193 guests.

In separate Denver-area restaurant news, Sean Huggard and Shucking Good Hospitality — the group behind Blue Island Oyster Bar & Seafood, Oliver's Italian, and Ash and Agave — announced a new concept called The Coastal Service planned for the Denver Tech Center at Belleview Avenue and Ulster Street, with an opening targeted for early 2027. The East Coast-inspired seafood and oyster bar is described as a sibling to Blue Island but with a distinct Nantucket-influenced identity.

Also in the metro area, True Food Kitchen opened its second Colorado location Monday in Boulder at 1755 29th St., within the Twenty Ninth Street Shopping Center. The health-focused chain already operates one location in Cherry Creek and now has 46 locations across 18 states.

stories.headline: Cardinals Rally Past Rockies 7-4 on Sunday; Colorado Now One Game From Worst Record in Majors
stories.summary:
The St. Louis Cardinals defeated the Colorado Rockies 7-4 on Sunday behind a three-run eighth inning that broke a 4-4 tie. JJ Wetherholt hit a go-ahead two-run double off Parker Mushinski, and Iván Herrera added an RBI single for his fourth hit of the game. Alec Burleson homered earlier, a 441-foot shot to right-center for his 19th of the season.

For Colorado, Hunter Goodman hit his 34th home run of the season to tie the game in the eighth before the Cardinals' rally, and also had an RBI single in the first. Brett Sullivan added a two-run homer in the sixth. Rockies reliever Tanner Gordon took the loss, charged with two runs and four hits in 3 1/3 innings.

The Rockies fell to 46-72 on the season, leaving them one game ahead of the Los Angeles Angels for the worst record in Major League Baseball. Colorado is scheduled to open a series Monday night in Arizona, with rookie right-hander Gabriel Hughes expected to take the mound.

stories.headline: Broncos Training Camp Day 9: Injured Players Return, Receiver Tez Bryant Continues to Turn Heads
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos returned to padded practice Monday for Day 9 of training camp after a day off Sunday, with a wave of injured players rejoining the field. Luke Wattenberg, Marvin Mims, Jordan Turner, Nate Adkins, Eyioma Uwazurike, and Sean Fresch Jr. all participated in practice in some capacity, providing a boost to a roster working through early-camp attrition.

Wide receiver Tez Bryant, a 2025 third-round pick out of Illinois, has been a standout of camp, drawing significant attention while veterans Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton have missed reps. Safety Talanoa Hufanga described cornerback Riley Moss as "one of the most athletic corners I've ever been around," as Moss continues to hold off first-round pick Jahdae Barron for a starting role.

The team also announced plans to host 14 free, open-to-the-public training camp practices at Broncos Park Powered by CommonSpirit, with capacity limited due to ongoing construction related to the Burnham Yard stadium project. Outside linebacker Jonah Elliss spoke with team media about his focus heading into his third NFL season.

topStory.headline: Trump Secretly Switched Planes in Turkey Amid Iranian Assassination Threat, Reports Say
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump was covertly moved off Air Force One and onto a smaller military aircraft minutes before departure from Ankara's international airport following last month's NATO summit, according to reporting by The Washington Post and CBS News. The operation was triggered by U.S. intelligence detecting a credible Iranian plot to fire a missile at the presidential aircraft as it departed Turkey on July 8. Trump was transferred to an Air Force C-32A using an airport catering truck, a vehicle typically used to load meals onto aircraft, while the switch was obscured from view.

Members of the traveling press corps and some White House staff remained aboard the legacy Air Force One, flying the same Ankara-to-RAF Mildenhall route as the president while unaware that Trump was not on board. Reporters were instructed to keep window shades in the press cabin closed during the departure; Trump later told reporters they were 'probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags that we have to deal with.' The Trump administration has not publicly disclosed that journalists and staffers were effectively flying as unwitting decoys. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a statement that 'there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.'

The deception was layered on top of a separate cover story Trump offered publicly before departure. Hours earlier, he announced he would fly home on the older, baby-blue Air Force One rather than the newer Qatari-donated and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet he had arrived on, saying the switch was 'for old time's sake' and would give U.S. troops stationed at RAF Mildenhall a chance to view the new plane. CBS News reported the Secret Service had in fact advised Trump to take the older aircraft for security reasons. Trump reunited with the newer Qatari-gifted plane at RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, eastern England, and flew the transatlantic leg back to Washington aboard it.

The revelations come against the backdrop of heightened U.S.-Iran tensions. During Trump's stay in Ankara, the U.S. military conducted significant strikes inside Iran following Iranian-linked attacks on commercial shipping. Trump himself acknowledged the threat environment during the summit, calling himself Iran's 'number one target.' Intelligence warnings about a possible attack on the president or his aircraft had been reported previously by The New York Times and CBS News, contributing to the decision to avoid using the new Qatari plane for the initial departure leg.

Multiple Trump administration officials expressed frustration Monday evening that the classified tactics and protective procedures had become public, warning that disclosure could limit the effectiveness of future presidential security operations. The Secret Service declined to comment, and the Air Force directed inquiries to the White House. Questions also persist about the security credentials of the new Qatari-donated aircraft; Trump said last month the plane would undergo additional upgrades, while Cheung maintained it remains 'a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level' security features.
